\begin{document}

\title{Can a Typed Decision Model Make the Decisions of a Database-and-Documents Assistant? An Evaluation
on Text-to-SQL, Routing, Page Finding and Answerability}

\titlerunning{Typed Decision Models in a Database-and-Documents Assistant}
\author{Neel Pradeep Jaiswal~(\ding{41}) \and Ronak Daniel Ramanathan \and Hima Deepthi Vankayalapati \and Elizabeth Jish Joy}
\authorrunning{N. P. Jaiswal et al.}
\institute{Mukesh Patel School of Technology, Management and Engineering, NMIMS, Mumbai, India\\
\email{neelpjaiswal@gmail.com, danielronak8105@gmail.com,}\\
\email{himadeepthi.vankayalapati@nmims.edu, jish.joy@nmims.edu}}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Assistants that answer questions from a SQL database and a document collection make several small decisions per
question: which source to use, which passage holds the answer, whether the database can answer at all, and whether a
generated query is wrong. These decisions are usually extra LLM calls. Typed decision models such as Jev instead
return probabilities for declared yes/no or multiple-choice questions, at a small fraction of the cost. We test
whether one can make these four decisions, on held-out data with baselines fixed in advance. On \N{sN} BIRD questions
with corrected labels, zero-shot Jev detects wrong SQL answers about as well as an LLM judge and a fine-tuned verifier
(AUROC \N{sAurocJev} against \N{sAurocJudge} and \N{sAurocMB}; neither gap is significant), but it is a poor
selector among candidate queries. Asked whether a schema holds the data a question needs, it
separates intact schemas from ones missing the needed columns with AUROC \N{rthreeAucCol}. On \N{rtwoN} new routing
questions over SEC financial data and filings, a single four-way choice routes \N{rtwoJevTwoAcc} correctly against
\N{rtwoLLMAcc} for an LLM router, a difference that is not significant, while the same decision posed as two independent yes/no questions routes
\N{rtwoJevYNAcc} correctly. On \N{roneN} new page-finding questions, re-ranking a cross-encoder's top 25 passages
with Jev puts the right filing page first \N{roneJBOne} of the time, against \N{roneBOne} for the cross-encoder's
own ranking.

\keywords{Text-to-SQL \and Retrieval-augmented generation \and Query routing \and Answer verification \and
Typed decision models \and Pre-registration}
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
A question-answering assistant over a company's data usually has two sources: a relational database for figures
and a document collection for everything the figures do not say. Before it writes an answer, such an assistant has
to decide several things. Should the question go to the database, the documents, both, or neither? Which of the
retrieved passages actually contains the answer? Does the database hold the data at all? And is the SQL it just
wrote likely to be wrong, so that it should try again? In most systems each of these decisions is another call to a
large language model (LLM), which costs time and money and fails in its own ways.

Typed decision models offer a cheaper path. Jev~\cite{typesafe2026jev}, released in September 2026, takes a piece of
text and one or more declared questions, either yes/no or a choice among named options, and returns a probability
for each answer without generating any text. Early evaluations report strong zero-shot accuracy and well-calibrated
choice probabilities on classification benchmarks~\cite{deusser2026jev}, competitive performance as a fast judge that
escalates uncertain cases to a stronger model~\cite{li2026jevjudge}, and clear failure modes: probabilities for logically related questions that do not fit
together~\cite{axioms2026,coherence2026}, and option names that outweigh the definitions attached to
them~\cite{sun2026typesafe,labels2026}. What has not been tested, as far as we found, is whether such a
model can make the decisions of a database-and-documents assistant, where the input is long (a schema, a page of a
filing) and some verdicts, such as whether a SQL query is right, have to be worked out rather than read off.

We evaluate Jev, zero-shot, in four such roles: (i)~detecting wrong SQL answers and deciding when to fall back to
other candidate queries; (ii)~deciding whether a database can answer a question; (iii)~routing a question between
a database and a filing library; and (iv)~finding the page of a long filing that answers a question. For each role
we compare it with the component it would replace. Three of the tests (answerability, routing, page finding) use
data built for them, with hypotheses, measures and baselines committed before the data existed; the SQL results
reuse candidates and labels from a companion study~\cite{companion2026warnings} and are descriptive.

The results draw a consistent line. Jev does well when the decision can be read off the text in front of it:
spotting SQL results that look wrong, telling whether a schema holds the needed columns, routing when the decision
is posed as one joint choice, and ranking a filing's passages. It does poorly when the decision must be derived or is
split up: choosing among plausible SQL queries, or routing posed as two independent yes/no questions. At a fraction
of a cent per question, this separates decision calls that can be moved off the LLM from those that should not.

\section{Related Work}
\paragraph{Typed decision models.} Since Jev's release, studies have measured it on general classification and
routing benchmarks~\cite{deusser2026jev}, as an LLM judge with confidence-based escalation~\cite{li2026jevjudge},
and at agent decision points such as tool choice and relevance gating, where it tied an open model on relevance
gating and neither beat chance at choosing between models~\cite{fastslow2026}. Others report that its probabilities
for related questions violate the probability axioms, over-endorsing single statements~\cite{axioms2026}, that
decomposing a decision changes its answers~\cite{coherence2026}, that it follows an option's name rather than the
rubric bound to it~\cite{sun2026typesafe,labels2026}, that accuracy moves by about five points with
wording~\cite{fastslow2026}, and that it rarely rejects when no option is right~\cite{missing2026}. We found no evaluation on text-to-SQL, on choosing between a database and documents, or
on ranking passages of long documents.

\paragraph{Verifying and selecting SQL.} LEVER~\cite{ni2023lever} re-ranks generated programs with a verifier that
reads their execution results; CHASE-SQL~\cite{pourreza2025chase} trains a selector over candidates from several
generators; GradeSQL~\cite{tritto2025gradesql} trains outcome reward models that beat majority voting.
Richardson~\cite{richardson2026predicts} compares signals that predict correctness, with LLM judges reaching AUROC
0.72--0.78. Cascades that escalate only when a scorer doubts an answer go back to FrugalGPT~\cite{chen2023frugalgpt}.
BIRD's original labels are wrong for about half of its Mini-Dev questions~\cite{jin2026annotation}, so we use the
corrected labels.

\paragraph{Routing and retrieval.} Adaptive-RAG~\cite{jeong2024adaptiverag} routes by predicted question complexity
and CRAG~\cite{yan2024crag} triggers corrective retrieval from an evaluator; Bai et al.~\cite{bai2025routing} route
between structured and unstructured sources with rules, and Dai et al.~\cite{dai2026xgboost} train an XGBoost router
that chooses document search, SQL or a refusal, with a confidence threshold but no route that uses both sources. Pointwise re-ranking by the probability of ``yes'' is
established~\cite{nogueira2020monot5,zhuang2023yesno}; cross-encoders such as BGE~\cite{chen2024bgem3} remain the standard second
stage.

\section{Setting and Method}\label{sec:method}
\paragraph{Pipeline.} The assistant under test answers from a PostgreSQL database and a library of PDF filings. An LLM SQL agent
writes a query, runs it read-only and retries on errors; document questions go through a two-round dense search
(\texttt{mxbai-embed-large}) returning up to 25 passages, optionally re-scored by a cross-encoder
(\texttt{bge-reranker-v2-m3}, reading each passage's filing title). The router (LLM or Jev) sees the question, a card
listing the database's tables and columns, and the five best-matching documents. Figure~\ref{fig:pipeline} shows where the four decisions sit.

\paragraph{Data.} SQL experiments use the BIRD Mini-Dev questions~\cite{li2023bird} held out from all development
(\N{sN} questions), scored against corrected gold queries~\cite{jin2026annotation}. Routing and page finding use a
database of 23 standard annual figures, taken from SEC XBRL filings, for 31 US companies, together with the 84
filings of FinanceBench's open sample~\cite{islam2023financebench} (44,918 passages). FinanceBench's own questions
served only for development; every result we report as confirmatory comes from questions built after the systems
were frozen.

\paragraph{Jev.} We call \texttt{jev-1.13} through OpenCode Zen at \$0.042 per million input tokens, always
zero-shot, with one fixed question per role. It is never fine-tuned, and its thresholds, where it needs one, are
fitted on separate data.

\paragraph{Pre-registration and statistics.} For the answerability, routing and page-finding tests, the hypotheses,
measures, tests and thresholds were committed to the repository before the data existed, with a change log for
anything altered later. The SQL study's protocol was committed before its verifiers, judge and decision models scored
the pool, but after the first answers had been scored in the companion study; its hypotheses concern the trained
verifier, and every Jev result in it is descriptive. Paired comparisons use the exact McNemar test (a sign-flip
permutation test when outcomes are fractional), one-sided for the SQL hypotheses and two-sided elsewhere; intervals
use a bootstrap with 2,000 resamples, and secondary hypotheses are Holm-corrected. We call two systems \emph{comparable}
only when the 95\% interval of their paired difference lies within $\pm$8 points.

\section{Detecting Wrong SQL and Deciding When to Fall Back}\label{sec:sql}
\paragraph{Setup.} For each question we pooled 21 candidate queries: GPT-5 mini's answer from the pipeline and five
further samples, the same six from gpt-oss-120b, and three samples each from DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Qwen3-Coder-30B and
GLM-5.3-Flash. The pipeline's own answer is the \emph{first answer}; it is correct for \N{sFirst} of questions, and
some candidate is correct for \N{sOracle}. Four kinds of checker see the question, the query and a preview of its
result: an LLM judge (Gemini 3.8 Flash, a 0--100 score); ModernBERT-base~\cite{warner2024modernbert} and Laya~\cite{laya2026}, a small
open decision model, each fine-tuned on execution-labelled candidates from other questions; and Jev, zero-shot, asked
``Does this SQL query and its result correctly answer the question?''. Trained checkers are trained, calibrated and
tested on rotating folds stratified by database, so every question is scored by a model that never saw it. The 393
questions, their labels and the first answers are those of the companion study~\cite{companion2026warnings}.

\paragraph{Pre-registered hypotheses.} H1: choosing the candidate with the highest ModernBERT score beats a majority
vote. H2: training on real candidates beats training on rule-based mutants of the reference query. H3: keeping the
first answer unless ModernBERT doubts it, and otherwise choosing from the pool, beats the first answer.

\paragraph{Detection.} Zero-shot Jev ranks wrong first answers about as well as the LLM judge and as ModernBERT
fine-tuned on thousands of labelled candidates (Table~\ref{tab:sql}): the judge's lead is \N{sGapJudgeJev}
(\N{sGapJudgeJevCI}) and Jev's lead over ModernBERT \N{sGapJevMB} (\N{sGapJevMBCI}), neither significant. Its scores are stable: rescoring 200 candidates gave a rank correlation of
\N{sJevRetest}, and scoring all 6,056 distinct candidates cost \N{sJevCost}.

\paragraph{Choosing.} Jev is a much weaker chooser. Taking the candidate it scores highest gives \N{sJevMax}, barely
above the first answer and below a plain majority vote. This fits the observation that decision models do well
when a verdict can be read off the text and poorly when it must be derived~\cite{li2026jevjudge}: noticing that a
result looks implausible is easier than telling which of two plausible queries is right.

\paragraph{Falling back.} H3 holds: the ModernBERT-triggered cascade raises accuracy from \N{sFirst} to \N{sPsix}
(gain \N{sPsixCI} points). H1 and H2 point the expected way but are not significant after Holm correction (H2 was before it). The cascade falls
back on \N{sPsixFall} of questions, so on average it generates \N{sPsixExtraTok} extra tokens per question instead of
the \N{sCostOtherTok} needed to build the whole pool every time, and its accuracy is close to always choosing from the
pool (\N{sPfive}). Because Jev doubts well but chooses poorly, we also tried it as the trigger in front of the best
chooser we found (ModernBERT's scores summed within clusters of agreeing candidates, \N{sPfivev} when used on every
question). With Jev's untuned rule ``fall back when $P(\text{correct})<0.5$'', accuracy reaches \N{sJthree} (gain
\N{sJthreeCI} points) while falling back on only \N{sJthreeFall} of questions (about \N{sJthreeExtraTok} extra tokens
per question); a threshold fitted like H3's gives \N{sJtwo} with \N{sJtwoFall} fallbacks, and Jev as the chooser
gains almost nothing (\N{sJone}). These analyses were decided after the pre-registered ones and are exploratory.

\section{Can the Database Answer This? Answerability with Hard Negatives}\label{sec:answerable}
\paragraph{Setup.} A SQL assistant should decline when its database lacks the data, rather than write a query that
returns something misleading. We took the \N{rthreeN} held-out BIRD questions whose reference query is correct and,
from each query's parse tree, the tables and columns it reads. Each question was paired with three schema cards: its
own database's full schema (answerable), the schema without the tables the query reads, and the schema without the
columns it reads (the hard case: the right tables are still there). Jev was asked ``Does the database described
contain the data needed to answer the question?'', with and without BIRD's hint, which often names columns.

\paragraph{Results.} Jev separates intact schemas from column-removed ones with AUROC \N{rthreeAucCol}
(\N{rthreeAucColCI}) with the hint and \N{rthreeAucColNoHint} (\N{rthreeAucColNoHintCI}) without it, and from
table-removed ones with \N{rthreeAucTab} and \N{rthreeAucTabNoHint}. A deployed gate must, however, almost never
refuse an answerable question. With thresholds fitted on one half of the questions to refuse at most 1\% of
answerable ones and applied to the other half, it refused \N{rthreeFalse} answerable questions while catching
\N{rthreeCatchCol} column-removed and \N{rthreeCatchTab} table-removed ones (with the hint); without the hint, it
caught \N{rthreeCatchColNoHint} and \N{rthreeCatchTabNoHint}. Ranking is strong, but at a strict false-refusal budget the gate catches about
half of the unanswerable cases with the hint and a third to a half without it. A simple baseline, the share of the
question's words that appear among the card's table and column names (not pre-registered), reaches AUROC
\N{rthreeLexCol} with the hint and \N{rthreeLexColNoHint} without it on the column-removed cards, so Jev's
judgement is far from word matching, especially when the hint does not name the columns. Because BIRD repeats some data across tables, a few
column-removed cards may still be answerable another way, so these figures are lower bounds.

\section{Routing Between a Database and Documents}\label{sec:routing}
\paragraph{Setup.} We built \N{rtwoN} new questions over the SEC database and the filing library, none from
FinanceBench, with labels fixed by construction: questions only the filings can answer (statements, and figures the
database does not hold, such as segment or quarterly results), questions either source can answer (a standard annual
figure for a year whose filing is in the library), questions only the database can answer in practice (across many
companies or years), questions that need both, and questions neither source can answer. Five routers, all frozen
before the set existed, were run once each: an LLM router (Qwen3.8-27B), a semantic router that takes the majority
label of the five most similar questions from an earlier labelled set, Jev asked one four-way choice question
(database only, documents only, both, neither) under two option wordings written earlier, and Jev asked two
independent yes/no questions (``does answering need the database?'', ``\ldots the documents?'') with thresholds fitted
on an earlier set.

\paragraph{Results.} Asked one choice question, Jev routed \N{rtwoJevTwoAcc} of the questions correctly with the
second wording and \N{rtwoJevOneAcc} with the first, against \N{rtwoLLMAcc} for the LLM router
(Table~\ref{tab:routing}); macro-averaged over the five classes the figures are \N{rtwoJevTwoMacro},
\N{rtwoJevOneMacro} and \N{rtwoLLMMacro}. The primary comparison, Jev's second wording against the LLM router, is not significant
(\N{rtwoHoneDiff} points, \N{rtwoHoneCI}, \N{rtwoHoneP}). Its interval reaches past our $\pm$8-point margin, so by
our rule the two are not shown comparable; the data are consistent with Jev being up to about two points worse or
up to ten better. The first
wording is comparable to the LLM router (\N{rtwoHthreeDiff} points, \N{rtwoHthreeCI}). Jev needed no LLM call and
took a median \N{rtwoJevTwoMs}\,s against \N{rtwoLLMMs}\,s.

The two routers fail in different places, and the difference matters. The LLM router sends most questions that
either source could answer to both sources (\N{rtwoLLMEither} correct): an unneeded search, but the answer is still
reached. Jev's choice gets all of those right and instead sends some documents-only questions to the database
(\N{rtwoJevTwoDocs}), almost all of them asking for a figure, such as a segment, quarterly or note figure, that the
database does not hold at that level of detail; those answers are lost. Counting a route as adequate when it
reaches every source the question needs, the LLM router reaches \N{rtwoLLMCovers} and Jev \N{rtwoJevTwoCovers}.

Posed as two independent yes/no questions, the same model routes \N{rtwoJevYNAcc} correctly, \N{rtwoHtwoDiff} points
below the single choice (\N{rtwoHtwoCI}, \N{rtwoHtwoP}). Its errors go both ways between the two-source class and
the rest: it sends \N{rtwoYNHybToDocs} two-source questions to the documents and \N{rtwoYNHybToSql} to the database,
and \N{rtwoYNEitherToHyb} either-source questions to both. The semantic router, which takes its labels from an earlier set's
examples, reaches only \N{rtwoSemAcc} (\N{rtwoHfourDiff} points against the LLM router, \N{rtwoHfourP}).

One failure is shared by the LLM router and all three Jev routers: each sent the ten questions about companies
that appear in neither source to the database (\N{rtwoLLMNeither} ``neither'' questions right for each, all misses
being these ten); the semantic router declined only \N{rtwoSemNeither}. The router sees the database's tables and columns, not which companies its rows cover, so a question about an
unknown company looks like an ordinary database question.

\paragraph{Telling the router what the database covers.} We then tested the fix this suggests, with the hypotheses,
question set and arms committed before the feature's code, the set and the runs existed. A switchable addition to the
database card lists, with no model call, every value of each text column with few distinct values (company names,
tickers, metric names, units) and the range of each date or year column. On 90 new questions that use the same three
phrasings in every class, so that only coverage tells them apart (30 about companies in neither source, 15 about
fiscal years 1998--2004, and 45 about companies and years the database holds), coverage raised the share of
uncovered questions that Jev declined from \N{rfourJevOffNeither} to \N{rfourJevOnNeither} (\N{rfourHoneDiff} points,
\N{rfourHoneCI}, \N{rfourHoneP}) and for the LLM router from \N{rfourLLMOffNeither} to \N{rfourLLMOnNeither}
(Holm-adjusted \N{rfourHtwoP}). Unknown companies were almost all caught (\N{rfourJevOnUnknown} and
\N{rfourLLMOnUnknown}); early years mostly were not (\N{rfourJevOnYears} and \N{rfourLLMOnYears}). That subclass does
not cleanly test year comparison: the card listed a curated table's range (from 2006) next to a raw table's (from
1989), so a 1998--2004 question could look covered.

On covered questions, Jev's routing could not get better or worse: it sent all 45 to the database in both arms, which
is acceptable for every one of them, so this check sits at its ceiling. The LLM router improved (\N{rfourHfourDiff}
points, \N{rfourHfourCI}, Holm-adjusted \N{rfourHfourP}): seeing that the database holds the company and the metric, it
stopped sending most single-figure questions to both sources. Re-run on the \N{rtwoN} routing questions above,
coverage raised Jev's accuracy from \N{rtwoJevTwoAcc} to \N{rtwoJevTwoCovAcc} (+\N{rtwoJevTwoCovW}/$-$\N{rtwoJevTwoCovL})
and the LLM router's from \N{rtwoLLMAcc} to \N{rtwoLLMCovAcc} (+\N{rtwoLLMCovW}/$-$\N{rtwoLLMCovL}); because those
questions motivated the change, this result is descriptive only. Each arm was run once.

\section{Finding the Right Page in Long Filings}\label{sec:pages}
\paragraph{Setup.} We sampled pages at random from the 84 filings, at most four per filing (330 pages from 83
filings, fewer than the 420 planned), (excluding FinanceBench's evidence pages,
a page set used earlier, and their neighbours), had an LLM write one specific question per page, and kept the first \N{roneN} that a second model
confirmed the page answers. For each question the two-round search returned 25 passages twice, once by
dense similarity and once re-scored by the cross-encoder. Four orders were compared: dense similarity (D), the
cross-encoder's scores (B), and Jev's probability that the passage ``contains the information needed to answer the
question'' applied to either list (JD, JB). Only the order differs within a list.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Page finding on \N{roneN} new questions: share whose source page is first, in the top 3, and in the top 8
(what the answer writer reads).}
\label{tab:pages}
\begin{tabular}{lrrr}
\toprule
Order & Page@1 & Page@3 & Page@8 \\
\midrule
Dense similarity (D) & \N{roneDOne} & \N{roneDThree} & \N{roneDEight} \\
Cross-encoder, GPU (B) & \N{roneBOne} & \N{roneBThree} & \N{roneBEight} \\
Jev over dense (JD) & \N{roneJDOne} & \N{roneJDThree} & \N{roneJDEight} \\
Jev over cross-encoder (JB) & \N{roneJBOne} & \N{roneJBThree} & \N{roneJBEight} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\paragraph{Results.} Re-ordering the cross-encoder's 25 passages by Jev put the source page first for \N{roneJBOne} of
questions, against \N{roneBOne} for the cross-encoder's own ranking (Table~\ref{tab:pages}; \N{roneHoneDiff} points,
\N{roneHoneCI}, \N{roneHoneP}), and it also raised the share with the source page in the top three (\N{roneHfourDiff}
points, \N{roneHfourP}). Without the GPU, over the dense list alone, Jev reached \N{roneJDOne}: \N{roneHthreeDiff}
points above dense similarity (\N{roneHthreeP}) and \N{roneHtwoDiff} points above the GPU cross-encoder, a difference
that falls just short of significance after correction (\N{roneHtwoCI}, \N{roneHtwoP}). The gain is at the top of the
list; whether the source page is anywhere among the eight passages the answer writer reads barely changes
(\N{roneJBEight} against \N{roneBEight}), because that depends on which passages the search found, not on their order.

On FinanceBench's own analyst-written questions, used for development, the gap was larger (\N{devFbJBOne} against
\N{devFbBOne}); on an earlier generated set it was smaller and not significant (\N{devOldJBOne} against
\N{devOldBOne}).

\paragraph{Cost and latency.} Scoring one question's 25 passages took Jev a median \N{roneJevMs}\,ms, eight
requests at a time, and cost \N{roneCost}. The two-round search took \N{roneDenseMs}\,ms without re-ranking and
\N{roneBgeMs}\,ms with the cross-encoder (measured while other jobs shared the GPU).

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
\paragraph{Reading off versus working out.} Li et al.\ found that Jev judges as well as a frontier model when a
verdict can be read off the text and falls behind when it must be derived~\cite{li2026jevjudge}. Our four roles
extend that distinction to a database-and-documents assistant. Where the answer is visible in the input, whether a passage states a figure, whether a schema has the needed
columns, whether a query's result looks plausible, it is not significantly worse than the component it would
replace, and on page ranking it improves on it. Where the answer has to be
worked out, which of two plausible SQL queries is right, it falls behind. SQL shows both sides of the line: a
wrong query often returns a result that looks wrong, which Jev can see, whereas choosing between two plausible
queries requires tracing what each computes. For a system designer this suggests using a decision model to \emph{trigger} work (fall
back, re-rank, decline) and leaving the \emph{choice} among generated answers to execution, voting or a trained
verifier.

\paragraph{Ask one question, not two.} The clearest design lesson is about how a decision is posed. Routing between a
database and documents is one decision with four outcomes; split into ``needs the database?'' and ``needs the
documents?'', each probability is reasonable on its own, but the pair does not separate questions that need both
sources from questions either source can answer. This fits the over-endorsement of single statements reported by Li
et al.~\cite{axioms2026}: both needs score high whenever either source is plausible. Posed as two questions, the
decision cost \N{rtwoHtwoDiff} points here. Posing the
whole decision as one choice removed it.

\paragraph{What the router cannot see.} A router shown only a database's columns cannot tell a question about an
entity the database holds from one about an entity it does not. Listing what the rows cover, which costs a few
read-only queries per database and no model call, fixed most unknown-entity errors for both routers. Period coverage
needs more care: our card showed both a curated table's range and a raw table's wider one, and a coverage line should
state the range of the data a question would actually be answered from.

\paragraph{Cost.} Every Jev decision in this paper cost well under a cent: \N{sJevCost} to score all 6,056 SQL
candidates, \N{roneCost} per question to re-rank 25 passages, and no LLM call to route. The constraint we met in
practice was the API's rate limit, not price.

\section{Threats to Validity}\label{sec:threats}
\paragraph{Generated questions.} The routing and page-finding questions were generated, from templates and by an
LLM, and may be cleaner than real users' questions. A page other than the source page may also answer a question,
which lowers every order's page accuracy alike.
\paragraph{How the questions were selected.} The second Jev wording was written after an earlier routing test had
shown the first wording's errors on documents-only questions; both were frozen before the new set existed. A question
writer that reasons before answering failed to return a usable figure question for some pages, so the figure
questions come from the pages where it did. BIRD's hints often name columns, which helps the answerability gate, so we
report it with and without them.
\paragraph{Labels and checks.} Routing labels are fixed by construction, and a page question was kept only when
a second model confirmed that its page answers it. No sample was labelled independently by hand, so errors in the
generated questions or their labels are not ruled out.
\paragraph{Wording.} Each Jev role used one fixed wording (two for routing). Accuracy of typed decision models
moves by about five points with wording~\cite{fastslow2026}; our two routing wordings differed by
\N{rtwoJevTwoAcc} against \N{rtwoJevOneAcc}, and single figures should be read with that band in mind.
\paragraph{One benchmark per role.} BIRD for SQL, one financial database and one filing library for the rest; English
only. Jev is a commercial model whose training data we do not know, and the models may have seen BIRD.
\paragraph{Hosts.} Models were reached through third-party APIs, some of which do not name their upstream provider;
the served model name is recorded for every call.
\paragraph{Earlier versions of two tests.} An earlier page-finding test compared Jev with the pipeline's display
order rather than the cross-encoder's ranking, and an earlier routing test reused questions from development. We
replaced both with the pre-registered tests reported here; the earlier results are in the repository.

\section{Conclusion}
Tested zero-shot on held-out data, a typed decision model detected wrong SQL answers about as well as an LLM judge,
judged whether a schema can answer a question with AUROC \N{rthreeAucCol}, routed \N{rtwoJevTwoAcc} of new questions
correctly without an LLM call, and put the right filing page first more often than a cross-encoder alone
(\N{roneJBOne} against \N{roneBOne}). It chose poorly among SQL candidates and failed when one routing decision was
split into two questions. Like the LLM router, it could not tell a question about an entity the database lacks from
an ordinary database question until the card listed what the rows cover. Decisions that can be read off the input
can be moved to such a model; decisions that must be worked out should stay where they are. Code, prompts,
pre-registrations, question sets and result files are available from the authors on request.
